1149.title: Like stars, like dew (section 32)
1149.hook: look on the world like stars, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud (Müller, section 32)
1149.howItsDone: Some Mahayana communities recite the closing verse of the Diamond Sutra on its own, at the end of chanting the sutra and at other times, as a short reminder that all that is made is passing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, views of self: what the Tathagata taught as a view of self is taught as no view, and so it's called a view. Your line: so-called views.

Dew covers the car in the driveway at six in the morning, the windshield beaded and silver. By the time the coffee's poured, the sun is over the fence, and by the time the keys are found, the glass is dry. Nobody saw it leave. The Diamond Sutra has spent weeks cutting: self, marks, merit, views. Now, in its last section, it stops cutting and hands over a few pictures, plain enough for a child, and says: look at the world like this.
screen: `DEW ON THE WINDSHIELD.` → `DRY BEFORE THE KEYS ARE FOUND.` → `THE BLADE HANDS OVER PICTURES.`

segments.voice: First, one last comparison. Someone fills worlds beyond measure with jewels and gives them all away. Someone else takes even four lines of this teaching, keeps them, and explains them to others. The second makes the greater merit. And how should it be explained? In the sutra's own way: without taking hold of the explaining, so that it's only called explaining. Then the verse. In paraphrase: look on all that is made like stars, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud. Each is something you can see. Stars shine all night and fade at dawn. A lamp burns only while the oil lasts. A magician's illusion. Dew, gone before the keys are found. A bubble. A dream that felt like a whole life. A flash of lightning. A cloud, changing shape as you watch. On day one hundred ninety-one, the Dhammapada asked you to look on the world as a bubble, as a mirage; here that same eye comes back. The verse doesn't say the world is fake. Dew is really dew; it really wets the glass. A few days ago the sutra warned against hearing emptiness as nothing. The verse holds both: real, and passing. Then the Buddha finishes, and Subhuti, the monks and nuns, the lay men and women, gods and humans and other beings all rejoice at what he has said. The Diamond Sutra began with an ordinary morning: a bowl, a meal, washed feet. It ends with a lamp, a bubble, and a crowd that is glad.

1150.title: The Lotus
1150.hook: the Lotus of the True Law: a sutra of parables, visions and one great promise
1150.carry: the lotus of the true law
1150.howItsDone: The Lotus Sutra is chanted, copied and studied in Mahayana communities in East Asia and beyond; Tiantai and Tendai Buddhists center their teaching on it, and in Nichiren Buddhism practitioners chant its title.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Diamond Sutra ended on its closing verse: look on the world like stars, like dew, like a bubble, like lightning. Your line: like dew, like lightning.

A lotus puts its roots down in pond mud, dark and soft. The stem climbs through murky water, and then, above the surface, the flower opens clean, as if it had never touched any of it. The Diamond Sutra was a blade: short, sharp, cutting away every grip. The next text on this path works in a different key. It tells stories. It stages visions the size of the sky. And it carries one promise so large that the people in the story don't believe it at first. It takes its name from that flower.
screen: `ROOTS IN THE MUD.` → `A FLOWER ABOVE THE WATER.` → `FROM A BLADE TO A STORY.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit the sutra is called the Saddharmapundarika. The scholar H. Kern, translating it into English, rendered the title as the Lotus of the True Law. Saddharma, the true Dharma, the true teaching. Pundarika, the lotus. So the title holds both the teaching and the flower. The image isn't new to this sutra. In a discourse in the Pali canon, the Buddha compares himself to a lotus: born in the water, grown up in the water, it rises above the water and stands unsoiled by it. So, he says, he was born and grew up in the world, yet lives unsoiled by it. Mud below, flower above, one plant. The Lotus is a sutra of parables. A father calling his children out of a burning house. A son who ran away and comes home not knowing he's the heir. A rain that falls on every kind of plant. A jewel sewn into a sleeping friend's robe. And it's a sutra of visions: a ray of light from the Buddha's brow, a jeweled stupa rising out of the earth, bodhisattvas springing up from the ground. Through it all runs one great claim: the Buddha's teachings, however many shapes they take, lead toward one goal, and those listening will themselves become Buddhas. Some East Asian schools, among them Tiantai in China and Tendai and Nichiren in Japan, place it at the center of their practice. On day one thousand you met Nichiren, for whom chanting the title itself is the practice. Over the coming weeks, this path walks through it story by story.

1151.title: The ray of light (Kern ch. 1)
1151.hook: a ray from the Buddha's brow lights up countless worlds; Manjushri says a great teaching is coming
1151.howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists who chant and study the Lotus Sutra begin with its opening scene on Vulture Peak, where the ray of light sets up everything that follows.

In a theater, a moment before the play, the house lights go down. Programs stop rustling. Phones go dark. Nobody has said a word, but everyone knows something is about to start. The Lotus Sutra opens with a moment like that, only the stage is a mountain and the light comes from the Buddha himself. He has just finished teaching. He goes silent, sits in deep meditation, and then something happens that nobody in the crowd can explain.
screen: `THE HOUSE LIGHTS GO DOWN.` → `A MOUNTAIN FOR A STAGE.` → `SOMETHING NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN.`

segments.voice: The Buddha is on the Vulture Peak, a mountain near the city of Rajagriha, with a vast crowd: monks and nuns, bodhisattvas, kings, gods and spirits. He finishes a teaching, sits cross-legged and goes into deep meditation. Flowers rain down from the sky. The ground trembles. Everyone falls silent and looks at him. From the tuft of white hair between his eyebrows, a single ray of light goes out toward the east, and in Kern's telling it lights up worlds upon worlds. In its light the crowd sees everything at once: beings in every kind of life, Buddhas teaching, bodhisattvas practicing, monuments to Buddhas long gone. The bodhisattva Maitreya wonders what this means, and so does everyone else. So he asks Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, who answers from memory. Long ago, a Buddha named Moon-Sun-Lamp did exactly this: the meditation, the flowers, the ray. And when he rose, he taught the Lotus of the True Law. So the same is about to happen now. A great teaching is coming. Then the twist. In that old story, Manjushri says, he himself was a bodhisattva named Varaprabha. And there was a disciple called Fame-Seeker, who loved gain and kept forgetting what he learned. Who was that? It was you, Maitreya. The one asking the question was once the slow student. The ray lights up worlds upon worlds, and it lands, gently, on him.

1152.title: Skillful means (Kern ch. 2)
1152.hook: the Buddhas teach in many ways, fitted to their hearers, toward one goal
1152.howItsDone: In Mahayana Buddhism, upaya, skillful means, is the teaching that Buddhas and bodhisattvas adapt their words to their hearers; chapter two of the Lotus Sutra is the classic place it is taught, and Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren teachers study it closely.

A kid at a kitchen table is stuck on fractions. Her aunt tries the textbook way. Blank look. She cuts an orange into pieces. Still nothing. Then she says: you and your friends split a pizza. And the face changes. Same fraction, third way of saying it. Nobody would call the aunt a liar for using pizza. She found the door this kid could walk through. The Lotus Sutra's second chapter is about that kind of teacher, on a very large scale.
screen: `STUCK ON FRACTIONS.` → `AN ORANGE, THEN A PIZZA.` → `THE DOOR THIS KID CAN USE.`

segments.voice: In chapter two the Buddha rises from his meditation and speaks, not to the crowd at large, but to Sariputra, the disciple known for wisdom. The knowledge of the Buddhas, he says, is deep and hard to understand, and then he says he will stop there. Sariputra asks him to go on. He declines. Sariputra asks again, then a third time, and only then does the Buddha agree. In Kern's translation, as he begins, a group in the assembly gets up and leaves, sure they've already understood. The Buddha lets them go. Not everyone is ready to hear everything at once, and he doesn't force it. The chapter's Sanskrit name is built on upaya, usually translated skillful means, or skill in means. The Buddhas teach in many ways: stories, comparisons, reasons, examples, each fitted to the people in front of them, because hearers differ in what they want and what they can take in. Here is the turn that makes the Lotus the Lotus. The many ways are not many destinations. The Buddhas appear in the world for one great purpose: to open the Buddha-knowledge to beings, show it to them, and lead them into it. The pizza and the orange were never the point. The fraction was. Some readers find upaya freeing, because it explains why Buddhist teaching looks so different from place to place. Others ask a sharper question, which the sutra takes up in the next chapter: if the teacher shapes the message, is that honest? A father with a burning house is coming to answer it.

Three travelers board a train through three different doors: front, middle and back. Each settles in and thinks of it as their own car. Then the conductor walks through and says: it's one train, going to one station. The doors were only so you could all get on. That's roughly the moment chapter two of the Lotus Sutra builds to, and it unsettles some of the people who had been walking longest.
screen: `THREE DOORS, THREE CARS.` → `IT WAS ONE TRAIN.` → `WHAT THE DOORS WERE FOR.`

segments.voice: Buddhist teaching speaks of different paths called vehicles, yana in Sanskrit, the word for a cart or carriage. The Lotus names three: the vehicle of the disciples who hear the teaching, the vehicle of those who awaken on their own, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas. Different travelers, different carts. Then, in chapter two, the Buddha tells Sariputra plainly: there is only one vehicle, the Buddha-vehicle. Not a second, not a third. The three were skillful means, offered because people differ in what they can hear. Underneath them the destination is the same for everyone: Buddhahood itself. That is ekayana, the one vehicle. And the sutra keeps widening the door, almost playfully. In Kern's translation the Buddha describes people who once made a small offering at a shrine, or bowed, or raised a hand, or said a single word of honor to the Buddha, even children who piled up sand as a stupa while they played. All of them, the sutra says, have reached awakening. The vehicle has room for the child in the sandbox. In the sutra's own story this is not a soft message. It tells disciples who had worked hard toward their own goal that the goal was a stopping place, not the end. Buddhist schools read this differently. Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren teachers put the one vehicle at the center of their teaching. The Lotus is not part of the Theravada canon, and Theravada teachers describe the path in their own terms. Today simply hears what the Lotus says, in its own voice. Tomorrow it becomes a story: a house, a fire, some children, and carts.

Smoke is already coming through the roof. The house is old, the beams are rotten, and there is only one door. Out in the yard stands the owner, a rich old man. Inside, his children are playing, so absorbed in their games they haven't noticed a thing. He shouts fire. They look up, puzzled, and go back to playing. They don't know what fire is. This is the parable the Buddha tells Sariputra in chapter three of the Lotus Sutra.
screen: `SMOKE THROUGH THE ROOF.` → `ONE DOOR, CHILDREN PLAYING.` → `HE SHOUTS FIRE. NOTHING.`

segments.voice: In Kern's telling, the father thinks of gathering the children in his strong arms and carrying them out. But the door is narrow, and they're running everywhere. So he tries something else. He knows what each child loves, and calls out: the toys you've always wanted are outside the door, carts drawn by goats, by deer, by bullocks. Come and get them. The children rush out together, pushing past each other, and are safe in the open air. In the yard they ask for their carts. The father gives each child the same thing, and it isn't any of the three. It's a great cart drawn by white bullocks, swift, high, decked with jewels and hung with bells, finer than anything they asked for. He is rich enough, the story says, and they're all equally his children, so why give any of them less? Now the Buddha asks Sariputra: did that father tell a lie? No, Sariputra answers. He saved their lives. Even if he'd given them nothing, he wouldn't have lied, because getting them out was the point. Then the Buddha explains. The house is the world, burning with suffering. The children are beings, absorbed in play. The three carts are the three vehicles; the great cart is the one vehicle. And the father is the Buddha, who uses skillful means because shouting the plain truth reaches no one who doesn't yet know what fire is. So here is the sutra's answer to whether shaping the message is honest: a promise made out of love, and kept more generously than anyone asked.

1155.title: Sariputra's promise (Kern ch. 3)
1155.hook: the wise Sariputra is told he too will become a Buddha
1155.howItsDone: In Lotus Sutra study, especially in the Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren schools, Sariputra's prediction in chapter three is read as opening the sutra's promises that disciples, and in time all beings, will become Buddhas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a father called his children out of a burning house with the promise of carts. Your line: out of the burning house.

A sealed envelope sits on a desk. Inside is a letter about your future, written by someone who knows you better than you know yourself. Would you open it? Chapter three of the Lotus Sutra opens with a moment like that, out loud, in front of everyone. Before the burning house is ever told, the Buddha speaks to the disciple who has been asking all along, and tells him something he had stopped hoping to hear.
screen: `A SEALED ENVELOPE.` → `A LETTER ABOUT YOUR FUTURE.` → `READ ALOUD, IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: The chapter actually begins here, before yesterday's parable. Sariputra stands, palms joined, glowing with happiness after what he heard in chapter two. In Kern's translation he tells the Buddha he had been troubled for a long time. Sitting alone, he would wonder why the bodhisattvas were promised Buddhahood and disciples like him were not. He had thought it was his own fault. Now the doubt is gone. The Buddha answers him in front of the whole assembly. Long ago, he says, I was already guiding you, though you had forgotten. And in a future age, after honoring many Buddhas and keeping the teaching, you yourself will become a Buddha. The sutra even gives the name: Padmaprabha, which can be rendered Lotus Light, with a land of his own, wide and well ordered. Sariputra was no beginner. In Buddhist memory he is the disciple known for wisdom, the one the Buddha had just chosen to speak to. If even he quietly carried the fear of being left out, the promise speaks to anyone who has assumed the best things were meant for other people. It won't be the last such promise. Over the coming chapters one disciple after another hears his future, and later women of the assembly hear theirs too. On day seven hundred seventy-eight you heard that the Lotus promises Buddhahood even to Devadatta. The one vehicle isn't left as a theory. It's said to a person, by name. Some readers in the Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren traditions dwell on these scenes because they make the teaching personal: every being, in this sutra's view, can wake up, even one who thought he'd missed his chance.
